title: La Vang (Vietnam)
hook: Catholics hiding from persecution in 1798 remember Mary appearing in the forest

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vailankanni: a shrine on India's coast where pilgrims bring their bodies' worries. Your line was our lady of good health. What did you do for someone's health? Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

A pot of leaves is boiling over a small fire, deep in a forest in the hills of central Vietnam. Around it sit families who have left their villages with whatever they could carry. They are Catholics, and in their country, at this time, being Catholic could cost you your home or your life. So they've come to the trees to hide. Some of them are sick with fever. There's no doctor, no medicine, and nowhere safer to go. At night they gather and pray the rosary together, quietly. The leaves in that pot have a story behind them, and Vietnamese Catholics still tell it. Today's word is the place in the forest.
screen: `A POT OF LEAVES OVER A FIRE.` → `CATHOLICS HIDING IN THE TREES.` → `SICK, WITH NOWHERE TO GO.`

segments.voice: First, the hiding. Tradition says that during a time of persecution, Catholics fled into the forest at La Vang. The Letter to the Hebrews describes believers like them, in the Douay-Rheims: "wandering in deserts, in mountains, and in dens, and in caves of the earth." A church without a building, praying under the trees. Second, the mother. Tradition says that as they prayed, a lady appeared among the branches, holding a child, with angels beside her. She didn't promise them their villages back, or tell them their persecutors would fall. She comforted them, and she told them what to do: gather the leaves from the trees around them and boil them as medicine for the sick. Third, the leaves. That small, practical instruction echoes the last chapter of the Bible. In John's vision of the heavenly city, a river runs through the street and the tree of life grows beside it, and "the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations." At La Vang, by the people's memory, the healing came from the ordinary trees they were hiding under. In the story, heaven doesn't lift them out of the forest. It meets them in it. Fourth, the keeping. Tradition says the people who survived remembered, and built a small chapel on the spot. Pilgrims still come, gathering under the trees as those families did. Like every apparition, La Vang asks no one to believe it. What it hands on is a picture: a mother finding her children exactly where they were hiding.
screen: `A CHURCH HIDING IN THE TREES.` · `A MOTHER WITH A CHILD, AND AN ANSWER.` · `LEAVES FOR HEALING.` · `REMEMBERED, AND BUILT.` · then, large: `THE LEAVES OF THE TREE WERE FOR THE HEALING OF THE NATIONS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Vietnam. Settle, and breathe. Bring the country to mind: its cities, its villages, its forests and coast. Then bring in its Catholics, past and present, including those who once prayed in hiding. Widen it to anyone in any country who has to hide what they believe today. Hold them gently, the way the families held the sick by that fire. If you pray, you can pray a decade of the rosary, as the people at La Vang did, for Vietnam. If you don't, simply hold its people in mind, one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
La Vang. The forest in Vietnam where, tradition says, Mary came to Catholics hiding from persecution and told them to boil the leaves as medicine. Today's word.
Your line: in the forest. Today, look for help that's already within reach where you are, and offer it to someone who feels stuck. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholics in Vietnam and abroad honor Our Lady of La Vang; pilgrims travel to the shrine at La Vang in central Vietnam to pray, and Vietnamese Catholic communities elsewhere keep images of her in their churches.

boil the leaves of these trees as medicine.

trapdoor: what you thought: a shrine somewhere in Vietnam.
what it means: the place where, tradition says, Mary came to hidden, sick Catholics and told them to boil the leaves of the forest for healing.
what a scholar hears: a story kept by memory rather than records, echoing Apocalypse 22:2's leaves for the healing of the nations.

notes: Editor: 'the people of Vietnam' narrowed to Vietnamese Catholics; the heaven line now framed as the story's; the chapel's founding put under 'tradition says' and the unsourced war-damage history cut (with its screen).
No year is spoken (the index hook's '1798' is kept off the voice under the claims rule); the persecution is left unnamed (often linked to the Tây Sơn period / Cảnh Thịnh's edict). Confirm.
Details of the tradition (the lady holding a child, with angels; telling them to boil leaves as medicine; a chapel built on the spot): confirm.
'Damaged and rebuilt through the country's wars' (the church at La Vang was destroyed in fighting and its ruins remain beside the newer shrine): confirm wording.
Hebrews 11:38 is applied to the La Vang Catholics as a description of believers in hiding, not as a claim that the text is about them; confirm.
The place-name 'La Vang' has popular etymologies (a kind of leaf; a cry); none is used.
Douay-Rheims wording of Hebrews 11:38 and Apocalypse 22:2: confirm.
